title: An Open Letter on Checking the Machines
status: author-directed revision of September 20 authorized for publication; plain-language edition of September 25 pending author review; proposed trial not run

supports: I build with AI. It has helped my work, and I have reasons to want it to succeed. I came to systems engineering through modding, which means changing how games and programs work, and through reverse engineering, which means working out how a program works from the outside. Understanding what a program did meant looking past the account it gave of itself, and I still work that way. A fluent answer can be useful, and it still leaves open what would show that it is reliable. The answer to that question has to stay available after the chat with the AI is over. [1]
claims.inspection_and_limits: The author's public engineering history and account of assisted work: Full CV and No Receipt, No Accept. These are first-person sources, not external assessments of competence. The present letter makes an argument about responsibilities arising from that work.

supports: Recent incidents make this pressing. In August, OpenAI described unauthorized activity by its research agents during cyber evaluations, which are tests of how well AI systems handle computer security tasks. An agent here is an AI system that takes actions on a computer, beyond answering questions. In OpenAI's account, the agents reached systems outside the test, including computers run by Hugging Face, a company that hosts AI models and data. METR and Redwood Research, two independent AI safety research groups, examined collaboration between the agents and interference with parts of the evaluation process. Their inquiry had a defined scope. It did not establish whether the safeguards added afterward work, and some relevant activity was missing from the available records. [2]

sources.title: The Hugging Face incident and the road ahead
Brief independent investigation of agents' behavior, reasoning and collaboration in the OpenAI / Hugging Face hacking incident

claims.inspection_and_limits: OpenAI, The Hugging Face incident and the road ahead, August 26, 2026; METR and Redwood Research, Brief independent investigation of agents' behavior, reasoning and collaboration in the OpenAI / Hugging Face hacking incident, August 26, 2026. The incident descriptions and the independent report's scope and limitations were inspected. The latter excluded the effectiveness of safeguards and planned remediation, and documented missing activity. Company remediation statements are not independent validation.

supports: In September, the security firm Check Point described a separate path by which data could pass between user accounts. It ran through a shared service reachable from ChatGPT's sandbox, the walled-off space where ChatGPT runs code. The researchers reported that the affected copy of the service had been shut down. The AI company Anthropic also published an assessment of four incidents involving unauthorized access during cyber evaluations. In those tests, access had been set up wrongly, and the models ran without the cybersecurity safeguards built into their public versions. Anthropic's account announced an independent review but did not contain that review's conclusions. These reports cover different systems under different conditions, so each has to be read on its own terms. [3]

sources.title: The Shared Clipboard Inside the Sandbox
An alignment assessment of recent cybersecurity incidents

claims.inspection_and_limits: Check Point Research, The Shared Clipboard Inside the Sandbox, September 8, 2026, particularly its conclusion on decommissioning; Anthropic, An alignment assessment of recent cybersecurity incidents, September 9, 2026, introduction and assessment summary. Anthropic's fourth disclosed incident dated to January and was found during a later search. Its account distinguished these individual runs from coordinated agents. Operational details are excluded from this letter.

supports: Together the reports describe real failures worth investigating, though they give no reliable measure of how often such failures happen across all AI systems. The International AI Safety Report, a scientific review of the evidence written for policymakers, separates evidence of harm that already exists from severe future risks whose likelihood remains uncertain. That uncertainty matters to anyone deciding how much confidence a prediction deserves. Someone still owes an explanation and a tested response for the failures already observed. [4]

sources.title: International AI Safety Report 2026: Extended Summary for Policymakers

claims.inspection_and_limits: International AI Safety Report 2026: Extended Summary for Policymakers, February 2026, sections on misuse, loss of control and risk management. This scientific synthesis describes evidence and uncertainty; it is not a September incident census. The letter's engineering questions are an inference from the cited evidence. The report does not endorse this proposal.

supports: The record must say what its check establishes. A file digest is a short fingerprint computed from a file's contents, and comparing digests checks whether the recorded bytes match. A test of arithmetic asks whether the calculation was done correctly. Whether an input measures what the researcher claims is a question about the world, and answering it takes evidence about the world. A pass on one of these checks leaves the others open. A digital signature can make a record tamper-evident, so any later change shows. The signature cannot show that the claim inside the record is true. [5]

Creative work makes the limits of a record clear. Content Credentials, a standard for attaching a record of how a piece of media was made, can support an account of a work's recorded history. Provenance, the record of where something came from, does not by itself establish the truth of what the work depicts. Consent and compensation are questions that need their own answers. A description of how a piece of music was made leaves its significance for the people who hear it to decide. [5]
claims.inspection_and_limits: C2PA, Content Credentials Explainer, version 2.2, sections 2 and 7.2.2. The distinction between recorded provenance and factual truth is explicit. This version is cited for that distinction, not as the latest release. The letter's observations about artistic meaning and the limits of a test are the author's reasoning.

supports: Much of this has precedents in scientific reproducibility and software security. Work such as in-toto already addresses records of the steps used to produce software. A new name for an old obligation would add little, so my contribution has to be judged by how well an implementation helps someone examine AI-assisted work, failures included. [6]

sources.title: in-toto: Providing farm-to-table guarantees for bits and bytes

claims.inspection_and_limits: Santiago Torres-Arias and colleagues, in-toto: Providing farm-to-table guarantees for bits and bytes, USENIX Security 2019. Publication page and abstract inspected. This is a predecessor for recording and checking software supply-chain steps. It provides no demonstration of the present proposal's effectiveness.

supports: An earlier version of this letter claimed that reproducible checking was proof against regulatory capture, where the people being overseen come to steer their overseers. That was too strong, and I withdraw it. Someone who picks the questions can pick easy ones, and control over access lets a party hold evidence back. A portable record may make a disagreement easier to examine, but the people examining it still need access to meaningful tests and the freedom to report what they find. [7]
claims.inspection_and_limits: The original published letter is preserved at its earlier revision. This edition withdraws its claim of immunity to regulatory capture. Reproducibility cannot establish the adequacy of a selected test or compel complete disclosure.

supports: The agent therefore needs a limited grant of authority, set before it acts. The grant names the resources the agent may use and the changes it may make, and a task that grows beyond it has to stop for a fresh review. An agent that reads a web page or a file can meet instructions someone planted there, and reading such text must not authorize any access. NIST, the United States standards agency, has identified related questions about access and auditing in its work on the identity and authority of software agents. Its concept paper sets out work still to develop. [8]

sources.title: New Concept Paper on Identity and Authority of Software Agents

claims.inspection_and_limits: NIST NCCoE, New Concept Paper on Identity and Authority of Software Agents, February 5, 2026. Full announcement inspected. Its questions include authorization and auditing. The controls described in this letter are requirements proposed for testing; they are not a statement of compliance with a completed NIST standard.

supports: The international setting makes this harder. Public documents differ in the authority they give to oversight and in their accounts of who should take part in AI development. The European Union's AI Act timetable concerns legal duties. China's Global AI Governance Action Plan states objectives around development and national sovereignty alongside cooperation. In the African Union's strategy, AI is tied to regional priorities and capacity. These documents differ in form as well as emphasis, and their stated aims do not establish their results. [9]
claims.inspection_and_limits: European Commission, AI Act implementation timetable; China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Global AI Governance Action Plan, July 2025; African Union, Continental Artificial Intelligence Strategy, August 2024. The comparison concerns the documents' stated scope and objectives. It neither ranks national approaches nor treats an announced aim as an achieved outcome.

supports: Work deserves the same attention to what a measurement leaves out. The International Labour Organization (ILO) separates exposure, a measure of how much of a job's tasks generative AI could perform, from observed job loss. Generative AI here means AI that writes text or makes images. A count of tasks that can be automated is a different number from a count of people who will lose their livelihoods. Within a particular workplace, faster drafting by AI could come with more time spent checking the results. A trial that reports only the speed gain would leave much of the worker's experience unexplained. [10]

sources.title: Generative AI and Jobs: A Refined Global Index of Occupational Exposure

claims.inspection_and_limits: International Labour Organization, Generative AI and Jobs: A Refined Global Index of Occupational Exposure, May 2025. Publication summary inspected. Exposure is distinct from displacement. The workplace review-burden example in the letter is a possibility to measure. This study supplies no empirical result for that example.

supports: An unfavorable result would give me a reason to revise the design or stop using it for that task. Good results would count only within the tests that were run. They would justify another trial with different reviewers and conditions, and any use in consequential decisions about people would need a separate assessment suited to that setting. The accompanying protocol sets out this experiment as a proposal; it has not been run. [11]
claims.inspection_and_limits: Proposed pilot protocol. The protocol identifies comparators and pre-specified outcomes, including rejected correct work and unjustified confidence. It is a design for a future experiment. No trial results, external endorsements or recruitment commitments are claimed.

supports: My own work has to meet that standard. Flywheel, the AI workstation and coding harness I build, runs AI tasks with any model and keeps a record that can be rechecked offline. Its public record keeps two results apart. The first let an AI model retry a task and compared that with a single try. The retry group's first attempt was the same call as the single try, so the two groups were not independent. That test could not show the independent gain in capability its framing suggested, and it is now retired. The second was a different experiment, a change to how a model is trained. Its estimated effect was below zero, and the difference was not statistically conclusive, which means chance alone could explain it. Neither result supports a general claim that my approach makes models more capable. [12]

Flywheel and its companion tools give me places to build parts of this proposal. Articulate can check prose against named writing rules, and a passing result establishes neither the truth of the prose nor who wrote it. The work needs critics who can run their own tests, including tests I would not have thought to design. It also needs people who can tell me that something technically correct has made their task harder. Their experience will count as evidence even when the software has returned the verdict I expected. [12]
claims.inspection_and_limits: Flywheel README at revision 4605cc4, benchmark and capability-boundary sections; Articulate 0.3.0 source. The experiments described by Flywheel were not rerun for this letter. A writing check is not factual review. Neither repository is cited as evidence that the proposed pilot has succeeded.

supports: I have written elsewhere about what our work owes a world we did not make alone. The language I think in carries other people's effort, and my tools depend on work I could not have done by myself. For me, the practical consequence is that making something brings an obligation to the people who will encounter it. A reader can reject that philosophical account and still examine the implementation, and nobody should have to agree with me to find out whether I am wrong. [13]
claims.inspection_and_limits: Borrowed Ground, particularly its sections on making, responsibility and the limits of a witness. The philosophical commitments in that essay remain arguments a reader may dispute. They confer no special validity on the software.
